soil-found-079.title: Soil solution: the water that is never just water
soil-found-079.text: The water in soil is never pure. It carries hundreds of dissolved substances, so soil scientists give it a more accurate name: the soil solution. It is the water held in the pores of soil, together with everything dissolved or suspended in it. These substances, organic and inorganic, sit in the liquid as ions or molecules. The solution is also a force of change. Water dissolves {{ref:soil-found-029}}, deposits new ones and washes material down through the soil, which makes it a critical agent in how soil develops. Its makeup shifts constantly. Soils wet and dry, plants take up {{ref:soil-fert-181}}, salts wash away, and acids or alkalis arrive. Plant foods held on {{ref:soil-found-040}} and on {{ref:soil-found-045}} buffer those swings, steadying the mix. One measure tracks the solution's acidity: {{ref:soil-found-014}} gauges its hydrogen ion activity, which governs how available those plant foods are.

soil-found-119.title: Mineralogy, the science of how minerals are built
soil-found-119.text: Talc sits at one end of a scale and diamond at the other. Mineralogy is the branch of geology that studies the chemistry, crystal structure and physical properties of {{ref:soil-found-029}}, optical ones included. It asks how minerals form, how to classify them, where they occur and how people use them. Some crystallize from molten rock deep in the crust; others grow as rock weathers at the surface or in soil. Identification starts with a hand sample. Hardness is a first clue, ranked on the Mohs scale from talc at 1 to diamond at 10. X-ray diffraction, shown in 1912, later revealed crystal structures.

soil-found-118.title: Calcite, the mineral that fizzes in acid
soil-found-118.text: A drop of acid on calcite starts a fizz, as the mineral dissolves and gives off carbon dioxide. Calcite is the most stable crystal form of calcium carbonate, CaCO3, and one of the {{ref:soil-found-034}}. It is very common, especially in {{ref:soil-form-147}}, and it marks hardness 3 on the Mohs scale. Water moving underground can either dissolve it or deposit it, depending on temperature, pH and the ions it carries. Less dissolved carbon dioxide makes calcite come out of solution. It also breaks a common rule: it grows less soluble as water warms.

soil-found-120.title: Phytoliths, the glass skeletons plants leave behind
soil-found-120.text: Plants drink stone. They take up dissolved silica from the soil as monosilicic acid, Si(OH)4, and it can make up 0.1% to 10% of their dry weight. Inside the tissue, the silica hardens into phytoliths: rigid, microscopic mineral deposits that often outlast the plant itself. They can survive in soils for thousands of years and are abundant in the fossil record from the Late Devonian onward. That durability makes them useful clues to past environments and changing vegetation. Carbon sealed inside them also resists decay for millennia. It builds up in soils, in stores that vary by species, biome, climate and soil.

soil-found-122.title: Weathering rinds, the stone clocks of old gravel
soil-found-122.text: A pebble's skin can tell its age. A weathering rind is a discolored, chemically altered outer layer on a rock fragment, formed as {{ref:soil-found-058}} works inward. Rinds grow on stones from pebbles to boulders, at the surface or buried in river, slope or glacial deposits, wherever air or shallow underground water reaches them. They are often enriched in iron, manganese and silica, and oxidized to yellowish or reddish hues. Thicker rinds on gravel of similar rock mean older deposits. Calibrated against radiocarbon-dated deposits, an age–thickness curve can date others, on the assumption that the relation is logarithmic.

soil-found-117.title: Core samples, columns of earth pulled out intact
soil-found-117.text: Dated cores of ocean floor, soil and ice have rewritten the history of the Pleistocene. A core sample is a cylinder of {{ref:soil-water-046}}, rock or soil, usually drilled out with a hollow tube. The material is pushed more or less intact into the tube, then removed in the laboratory for study. Hand coring with a simple tube or piston corer is cheap and quick, but in clay soils it reaches only a few decimeters. Cores are rarely perfect. Tools often crack them and lose weaker layers, which complicates reading them. Drilling that brings up only cuttings yields no undisturbed core at all.

soil-found-116.title: Trial pits: digging down before building up
soil-found-116.text: Before a building goes up, someone often digs a hole. A trial pit, also called a test pit, is an excavation dug to study or sample what lies below the surface. Most are dug for a site investigation or a soil or geological survey. A pit reveals a site's geology and how deep the water stands, and it lays bare the layers described in {{ref:soil-found-001}}. Pits usually run 1 to 4 meters deep, dug by hand or with a mechanical digger. Regulations require any pit deeper than 1.2 meters to be secured against collapse if people will enter it.
